clinicalPearls: Non-progressive rod-system disorder presenting from birth with night blindness, and often nystagmus, myopia and reduced acuity, especially in X-linked forms
A normal-appearing fundus in a patient with lifelong nyctalopia is a strong clue to the diagnosis

The Schubert-Bornschein type shows a characteristic electronegative electroretinogram, where the b-wave is reduced below the a-wave under scotopic bright-flash conditions, reflecting impaired signalling from photoreceptors to bipolar cells
It subdivides into complete (ON-bipolar dysfunction, for example NYX, GRM6, TRPM1) and incomplete (ON and OFF pathway, for example CACNA1F) forms distinguished by detailed electrophysiology
The Riggs type shows reduced rod a-wave amplitude without the electronegative configuration, reflecting a phototransduction defect
Inheritance is commonly X-linked (NYX, CACNA1F) but autosomal recessive and dominant forms exist
The condition is stationary, so management is refractive correction, low-vision advice where needed, and genetic counselling rather than treatment of progression
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital stationary night blindness is caused by mutations that disrupt rod-mediated signal transmission. In the common Schubert-Bornschein group, defects in genes controlling the photoreceptor-to-bipolar synapse (NYX, GRM6, TRPM1 for the complete form; CACNA1F for the incomplete form) impair transmission to depolarising bipolar cells, producing the electronegative electroretinogram despite preserved photoreceptor phototransduction. In the rarer Riggs type, the primary defect is in rod phototransduction itself, reducing the rod a-wave. Because the abnormality is developmental and non-degenerative, visual function remains stable over life.
additionalDifferentials: Retinitis pigmentosa and other progressive rod-cone dystrophies
Oguchi disease and fundus albipunctatus (other stationary night-blindness disorders)
Melanoma-associated or other autoimmune retinopathy causing negative electroretinogram
additionalInvestigations: Full-field electroretinography to detect an electronegative waveform and classify complete versus incomplete forms
Detailed ON/OFF and S-cone electroretinographic protocols for subtyping
Dark adaptometry to quantify the rod threshold defect
Refraction and assessment for nystagmus and myopia
Molecular genetic testing (NYX, CACNA1F, GRM6, TRPM1 and others)
Fundus examination and imaging to confirm an otherwise normal retina
redFlags: Documented progression of field loss or fundus change, which should prompt reconsideration of a degenerative diagnosis
Systemic features or malabsorption suggesting acquired vitamin A deficiency
Sudden onset of night blindness later in life indicating an acquired cause such as autoimmune retinopathy
New maculopathy raising suspicion of an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: By definition the disorder is stationary; night vision and acuity remain stable throughout life, though associated myopia and nystagmus may limit best-corrected acuity.
pitfalls: Mislabelling a stable patient as having progressive retinitis pigmentosa
Overlooking the electronegative electroretinogram or failing to perform electrophysiology in a patient with lifelong nyctalopia and a normal fundus
Confusing acquired night blindness (vitamin A deficiency, autoimmune retinopathy) with the congenital disorder
Not distinguishing complete from incomplete forms, which carry different associated features
